subject: community-medicine
title: Water Supply: Wholesomeness Standards and Sand Filtration Methods

steps.title: Safe and wholesome water criteria
steps.tx: In environmental sanitation, potable drinking water must satisfy four fundamental criteria to be classified as **safe and wholesome water**. It must be completely free from pathogenic microorganisms; free from toxic chemical substances and heavy metals; aesthetically pleasant, clear, colorless and odorless; and usable for domestic culinary and hygiene purposes without corroding plumbing or posing chronic toxicity hazards to human health.
steps.say: Safe and wholesome water is completely free from disease-causing germs and toxic chemicals. It is crystal clear, pleasant to taste, and odorless for all domestic cooking and drinking.

rows: Zero E. coli / thermotolerant coliforms per 100 ml
Arsenic < 0.01 mg/L, Fluoride < 1.0 mg/L, Lead < 0.01 mg/L
Turbidity < 1 NTU, pleasant taste, zero odor
Aesthetic rejection drives consumers to unsafe sources
Total dissolved solids < 500 mg/L, moderate hardness
Scale encrustation in pipes or heavy metal leaching

steps.title: Water-borne versus water-washed disease transmission
steps.tx: Public health engineers classify water-associated infections into four distinct transmission mechanisms: water-borne, water-washed, water-based, and water-related insect vectors. Water-borne diseases (cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A) result from ingesting faecally contaminated drinking water; **water-washed infection risks** (trachoma, scabies, bacillary dysentery) result from acute scarcity of water for personal washing, where providing abundant volume is more protective than chemical purity.
steps.say: Water-borne diseases are caught by swallowing contaminated water. Water-washed infections like scabies and eye trachoma happen when water is too scarce for people to wash their skin and clothes.

rows: Ingesting water contaminated with human or animal faeces
Cholera, typhoid fever, hepatitis A and E, amoebiasis
Inadequate water volume for personal body and facial hygiene

Biting insects that breed in or near water bodies

steps.title: Large-scale water purification sequence
steps.tx: To transform turbid river or lake surface water into potable supply, municipal waterworks execute a structured **municipal water treatment sequence** comprising four sequential unit operations: storage and plain sedimentation, chemical coagulation and flocculation, sand filtration, and final chemical disinfection with chlorine. Storage permits natural physical settling of suspended silt while bacterial oxidation reduces organic matter and pathogenic bacterial counts by ninety percent over two weeks.
steps.say: Municipal waterworks purify surface water in four stages: reservoir settling, chemical coagulation with alum, sand filtration, and final disinfection with chlorine to kill all surviving microbes.

nodes.label: Chemical coagulation with alum and flocculation
Rapid or slow sand bed filtration

steps.title: Slow sand filters: biological filtration
steps.tx: Invented by James Simpson in 1829, the classical **slow sand filter installation** purifies water through physical straining, sedimentation, adsorption, and extensive biological oxidation within a slow gravity filtration bed. Operating at low filtration rates between zero point one and zero point four metres per hour (two to five million gallons per acre daily), it requires no pre-coagulation chemicals, relying on natural biological mechanisms.
steps.say: Slow sand filters treat water at low speed through fine sand. They need no added chemicals because a natural living biological skin on the sand digests and destroys passing bacteria.

rows: Scraping upper 1 to 2 cm sand layer
Backwashing with compressed air and water

steps.title: The vital layer: Schmutzdecke formation
steps.tx: The heart of slow sand purification is the **Schmutzdecke biological layer**, also known as the vital layer or zoogleal film, which forms on the top few millimetres of the sand bed after several days of continuous filtration. Composed of living algae, plankton, diatoms, protozoa, and aerobic saprophytic bacteria, this slimy biological carpet traps microscopic particles and metabolically consumes passing pathogenic bacteria, achieving ninety-nine point nine percent microbial clearance.
steps.say: The Schmutzdecke is a living biological skin of algae and beneficial bacteria growing on top of the sand. It digests organic waste and eats passing disease-causing bacteria, sterilising the water.

nodes.label: Algae, diatoms and bacteria form slimy zoogleal layer

steps.title: Slow sand filter cleaning: scraping the bed
steps.tx: As the biological film thickens and accumulates trapped silt, frictional resistance impedes water flow, causing the loss of head to reach its critical threshold of one point two metres. Plant operators execute **slow sand filter scraping**, carefully draining the water bed, scraping off the top one to two centimetres of clogged sand with flat shovels, and allowing a new vital layer to regenerate over two to three days before resuming treated water delivery.
steps.say: When the sand filter gets clogged, workers drain the bed and scrape off the top two centimetres of dirty sand. The filter must run for three days to regrow its living skin before water is used.

nodes.label: Loss of head reaches 1.2 metres threshold
Drain supernatant water below sand surface
Scrape top 1 to 2 cm of dirty sand with shovels
Filter-to-waste for 48 hours until new Schmutzdecke matures

steps.title: Rapid sand filters: Paterson and mechanical design
steps.tx: Because slow sand filters require vast land acreage and cannot handle highly turbid river floodwaters, modern metropolitan water authorities install the compact **rapid sand filter installation**, exemplified by the Paterson gravity filter. Operating at filtration velocities fifty times faster than slow filters, it treats five to fifteen metres per hour using coarse sand grains, demanding prior chemical coagulation with alum and rapid mechanical flocculation to precipitate suspended mud.
steps.say: Rapid sand filters treat fifty times more water per hour than slow filters on a fraction of the land. They use coarser sand and require alum chemical coagulation to handle muddy river water.

points: Handles raw water turbidity up to 500 NTU
Easily scaled up for large metropolitan cities

right.title: Operational demands
points: Continuous electrical power for backwash pumps

steps.title: Backwashing the rapid sand filter
steps.tx: When rapid sand filters clog every twenty-four to forty-eight hours, cleaning is achieved through mechanical **rapid sand filter backwashing**, reversing the flow of clean filtered water from the underdrain upward through the sand bed under pressure. Compressed air is bubbled upward to agitate and scrub sand grains, followed by high-velocity wash water that expands the bed and flushes dislodged floc into surface wash troughs, completing cleaning in fifteen minutes.
steps.say: Rapid filters are cleaned by backwashing, forcing clean water and compressed air backward up through the sand bed. The bubbling wash flushes out trapped dirt in fifteen minutes without manual shoveling.

High-velocity upward wash water flushes trapped sludge
Back to forward filtration within 15 minutes

steps.title: Comparison of slow and rapid sand filtration
steps.tx: Public health engineers conduct a thorough **sand filtration comparison** when choosing water treatment systems based on land availability, raw water turbidity, capital resources, and technical skill. Slow sand filters provide biological purity without chemicals, making them ideal for rural communities with low turbidity water; rapid sand filters offer small physical footprints and automated operation, making them the standard choice for densely populated industrial municipalities.
steps.say: Slow sand filters are ideal for rural towns with clear water, needing no chemicals or electricity. Rapid sand filters suit crowded cities, handling muddy river water through compact machinery.

rows: High capital cost, skilled electrical operators
